## Introduction

### Overview

In Exercise 1, you'll practice with the GitHub material from last week
that wasn't part of Graded Assignment 2.
In Exercises 2-5, you'll practice with this week's material:
you'll explore OSC's login and compute nodes, plan resource usage,
and find and run software with modules and containers.

### Setting up

1. Start a VS Code session through OSC OnDemand in the folder
   `/fs/ess/PAS3493/people/<user>`.
2. For Exercises 2-5, navigate to the `week06` dir that you used in the
   [w6b lecture](./w6b_software.qmd).
3. _Optional_: Create and use a Markdown file to keep notes on what you're doing.

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

::: callout-tip
#### Lecture page exercises
Make sure to do any of the exercises on this week's lecture pages that we did
not do in class.
Also, if you struggled with any of the exercises we did do in class,
go over those again.
:::

## Exercise 1: GitHub

1. Go to the GitHub website, log in, and create a new GitHub repository.
   This will be the remote counterpart of the Git repo you made as
   part of last week's assignment.
   You can give the GitHub repo any name you want.

2. In the terminal in VS Code, navigate to your dir for last week's assignment.
   Then, use Git commands to set up a connection between the Git repo
   and the GitHub counterpart.

3. Push your local repo to the online counterpart.

4. Explore your repo on GitHub.
   Does your `README.md` render well? Can you see all your commits?

5. Open a GitHub Issue for your repo:
   on the GitHub page for your repo, click the Issues tab and then "New Issue".
   In the box where you can type your issue (i.e., the body), tag both instructors.
   (Don't try to do this in the title of the issue, it only works in the body.)
   For example:

   ```markdown
   Hey @jelmerp and @kstarr791, can you please take a look at my repo?
   ```

   _(You will use this approach to "hand in" the remaining assignments for this course.)_

6. Back in VS Code, add a line to your `README.md` that mentions you created a
   GitHub repo on today's date, adding the repo's URL.

7. Commit the change to `README.md` to your Git repo.

8. Push to the remote and check that the changes were applied in the online repo.

## Exercise 2: Login versus compute nodes

1. In your VS Code terminal, run the command `hostname`,
   which prints the name of the node (computer) that you're on.

2. In OnDemand, open a shell via "Clusters" > "Cardinal Shell Access",
   and run `hostname` there, too.

3. Which of the two is a login node, and which one is a compute node?
   How can you tell, and why is your VS Code session on that type of node?

4. In the Cardinal shell, navigate to `/fs/ess/PAS3493/people/$USER` and list its contents.
   Do you see the same files as in VS Code, even if your VS Code session is running
   on a different cluster? Why?

## Exercise 3: Planning resources

You have RNA-Seq data for 40 samples, and you want to align the reads
with an alignment program.
On a test sample, the program ran for 30 minutes with 16 reserved cores.

1. If you align all 40 samples one after the other, with 16 cores each,
   how many core hours will this use?

2. You then read in the program's documentation that it doesn't benefit
   from more than 8 cores.
   How many of the core hours from question 1 were wasted?

3. To be safe, you set a time limit of 2 hours per sample, rather than 45 minutes.
   Does that make your jobs more expensive?

## Exercise 4: The software version you need

You want to compare your results with those of a published study
that used FastQC version **0.11.9**,
so you want to use that exact version.

1. Is FastQC 0.11.9 available as an OSC module?

2. Get a Seqera container with FastQC 0.11.9,
   and assign its URL to a variable called `FASTQC_OLD_CONTAINER`.

3. Check the FastQC version using the container.
   Then, in the same terminal, load the `fastqc/0.12.1` module and run `fastqc -v`
   both with and without the container.
   Which version do you get in each case, and why?

## Exercise 5: Summarize FastQC results with MultiQC

As you saw in class, the program MultiQC is not available as an OSC module.
MultiQC summarizes the results of FastQC and many other bioinformatics programs,
across samples, in a single report.

1. Using the FastQC module, run FastQC on _both_ FASTQ files of sample S64
   with a _single_ command, writing the output to `results/fastqc`.
   (Hint: FastQC accepts multiple FASTQ files, and you can use a glob.)

2. Get a Seqera container with MultiQC,
   assign its URL to a variable called `MULTIQC_CONTAINER`,
   and use the container to run `multiqc --version`.

3. Using MultiQC's help info, figure out how to run MultiQC on your `results/fastqc` dir,
   with its output files in `results/multiqc`. Then, run it.

4. List the output files, then download the HTML report and open it.
   How does it compare to the individual FastQC reports?

5. _Bonus_: Get a single Seqera container with both FastQC and MultiQC,
   and check that you can run both programs with it.

## Solutions

### Exercise 1

<details><summary>**2.** Navigate, then set up a connection to the online repo</summary>

```bash
cd GA2

# (replace <SSH-URL-to-repo> with your actual SSH (not HTTPS!) URL)
git remote add origin <SSH-URL-to-repo>
```

</details>

<details><summary>**3.** Push your local repo to the online one you just created</summary>

When you push to a remote repo for the first time,
you need to add the `-u origin main` part:

```bash
git push -u origin main
```
</details>

<details><summary>**7.** Commit the change you made to `README.md`</summary>

```bash
git add README.md
git commit -m "Update README with GitHub repo information"
```
</details>

<details><summary>**8.** Push to the remote</summary>

Since you've pushed to this remote before, a simple `git push` works:

```bash
git push
```
</details>

### Exercise 2

<details><summary>**1.-2.** `hostname` in VS Code and in the Cardinal shell</summary>

In VS Code:

```bash
hostname
```
```bash-out
p0231.ten.osc.edu
```

In the Cardinal shell:

```bash
hostname
```
```bash-out
cardinal-login01.hpc.osc.edu
```

_(Your exact node names will differ.)_

</details>

<details><summary>**3.** Login node versus compute node</summary>

The Cardinal shell is on a **login node**, as you can tell from the `login` in its name.
VS Code is on a **compute node**:
when you start a Code Server session, you request a compute job,
and the job scheduler assigns your session to a compute node.

</details>

<details><summary>**4.** Files across clusters</summary>

```bash
cd /fs/ess/PAS3493/people/$USER
ls
```

You see the same files,
because all of OSC's nodes and clusters share the same file systems.

</details>

### Exercise 3

<details><summary>**1.** Core hours for all samples</summary>

16 cores × 0.5 hours × 40 samples = **320 core hours**.

</details>

<details><summary>**2.** Wasted core hours</summary>

Only 8 of the 16 reserved cores were used,
so the other 8 were idle:
8 cores × 0.5 hours × 40 samples = **160 core hours**,
or half of the total!

</details>

<details><summary>**3.** A generous time limit</summary>

No: OSC only bills for the time a job actually ran,
so each run still costs 30 minutes' worth of core hours.
On the other hand, a time limit that is _too short_ would be a problem,
because your job would be stopped before the program finished.

</details>

### Exercise 4

<details><summary>**1.** Is FastQC 0.11.9 available as a module?</summary>

No, only version 0.12.1 is available:

```bash
module spider fastqc
```
```bash-out
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  fastqc: fastqc/0.12.1
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

    This module can be loaded directly: module load fastqc/0.12.1
```

</details>

<details><summary>**2.** Get a container with FastQC 0.11.9</summary>

At <https://seqera.io/containers>, search for `fastqc`,
select version `0.11.9` in the dropdown menu of the `bioconda::fastqc` hit,
and then proceed as shown in the lecture
(don't forget to select `Singularity`).

Your URL will look like
`oras://community.wave.seqera.io/library/fastqc:0.11.9--<hash>`:

```bash
FASTQC_OLD_CONTAINER=oras://community.wave.seqera.io/library/fastqc:0.11.9--<hash>
```

</details>

<details><summary>**3.** Which version do you get?</summary>

```bash
apptainer exec "$FASTQC_OLD_CONTAINER" fastqc -v
```
```bash-out
FastQC v0.11.9
```

```bash
module load fastqc/0.12.1

apptainer exec "$FASTQC_OLD_CONTAINER" fastqc -v
fastqc -v
```
```bash-out
FastQC v0.11.9
FastQC v0.12.1
```

(The `INFO:` lines printed by Apptainer are not shown above.)

With the container, you always get version 0.11.9,
regardless of which modules are loaded:
the container uses the software installed inside it.
Without the container, you get the version from the loaded module.

</details>

### Exercise 5

<details><summary>**1.** Run FastQC on both S64 files</summary>

```bash
module load fastqc/0.12.1
fastqc --outdir results/fastqc ../garrigos/fastq/S64_R*.fastq.gz
```

</details>

<details><summary>**2.** Get a MultiQC container and check the version</summary>

At <https://seqera.io/containers>, search for `multiqc`,
add the `bioconda::multiqc` hit, and proceed as shown in the lecture.
Your URL will look like
`oras://community.wave.seqera.io/library/multiqc:<version>--<hash>`:

```bash
MULTIQC_CONTAINER=oras://community.wave.seqera.io/library/multiqc:<version>--<hash>
apptainer exec "$MULTIQC_CONTAINER" multiqc --version
```

</details>

<details><summary>**3.** Run MultiQC</summary>

MultiQC's help info shows that it takes a dir with results as an argument,
and that it has an option `-o`/`--outdir` to specify the output dir:

```bash
apptainer exec "$MULTIQC_CONTAINER" multiqc --help
```

So, you can run MultiQC as follows ---
unlike FastQC, MultiQC will create the output dir for you:

```bash
apptainer exec "$MULTIQC_CONTAINER" \
  multiqc --outdir results/multiqc results/fastqc
```

</details>

<details><summary>**4.** MultiQC output</summary>

```bash
ls -lh results/multiqc
```

The main output is the HTML report, `multiqc_report.html`,
and there is also a dir `multiqc_data` with tables of the summarized data.

The report shows the FastQC results for all files together,
for example with the per-base quality scores of all files in a single graph.
This makes it much easier to compare files and to spot outliers
than going through individual FastQC reports ---
especially when you have dozens of samples.

</details>

<details><summary>**5.** _Bonus_: A container with both FastQC and MultiQC</summary>

At <https://seqera.io/containers>, add both `bioconda::fastqc` and
`bioconda::multiqc` before clicking `Get Container`.
Then:

```bash
QC_CONTAINER=oras://community.wave.seqera.io/library/fastqc_multiqc:<hash>
apptainer exec "$QC_CONTAINER" fastqc -v
apptainer exec "$QC_CONTAINER" multiqc --version
```

</details>
